title: How proposed settlement rules would affect women, children and refugees
label: 4 November 2026 · Equalities impacts of routes to settlement
summary: The panel of immigration, children’s and women’s rights experts told the Women and Equalities Committee that the Government’s earned-settlement proposals will disproportionately harm migrant women, disabled people, refugees and many children. They warned retrospective application, earnings-based thresholds and long 10–30 year routes would deepen inequality, increase destitution and undermine social cohesion. The witnesses urged the Government to publish impact assessments, protect vulnerable groups, fund legal help and clarify routes for children and care leavers.

chapters.title: Short overview: what witnesses think
chapters.takeaway: Experts agree the package will widen inequality, hurt vulnerable people and damage trust unless key exemptions and assessments are made.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Now that the Government has published earned settlement and wider asylum changes, please give us a short overview of your main concerns about equalities impacts.

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: The package promotes intersectional discrimination: migrant women—often Black or minoritised, lower paid and more likely to be abused—will be hit hard. It risks a 'Windrush effect' of alienation and makes settlement feel like a privilege, not a right.

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: For children, long routes are not in their best interests. While the response keeps some five-year options for certain children, many families and single parents face indefinite limbo, which affects schools, health and housing.

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: From a business and individual view, many people earning under the new thresholds are already 'just about managing'. Delaying settlement raises costs for families and employers and undermines the UK's reputation for attracting talent.

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: Half a million is the Government’s floor figure who will wait longer; other counts put it much higher. The scheme is earnings-focused, so it embeds gender, racial and disability pay gaps and will be costly and administratively complex.

chapters.title: What the Government says it wants and whether it will work
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses say the reforms aim to 'reward contribution' and deter irregular entry, but evidence suggests they won't deliver savings, integration or fairness.

turns.speaker: Dame Nia Griffith
turns.text: What objectives do you think the Government are trying to achieve, and will the proposals reach them?

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: The aims appear to be: make settlement 'earned', reward fiscal contribution, promote integration, punish non-compliance and reduce net migration. In practice, the rules add tests—earnings, English, Life in the UK, criminal and debt checks—so settlement is not automatic.

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: Savings would mostly come from delaying benefit access; that's short-term and might cost more if people leave or need local services. Integration suffers when status is insecure—housing, work and education become unstable.

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: The Government talks about compliance, but the changes mostly affect already compliant, low-paid people—the 'JAMs'—which undermines the aim of targeting abuse or non-compliance.

turns.speaker: Dame Nia Griffith
turns.text: Is there clarity on how many people face 10 years or more and which groups are worst affected?

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: Officially 500,000, but figures look higher—possibly over 1 million. Sectors hit include hospitality, retail, engineering and defence. Regionally, lower wages mean more people fall under longer routes, harming places such as Scotland.

chapters.title: Women, domestic abuse and vulnerable migrants
chapters.takeaway: Earnings tests, limited exemptions and retrospective rules will trap some victims of abuse in dangerous situations and increase destitution.

turns.speaker: Nadia Whittome
turns.text: Dr Siddiqui, how will these proposals affect women's vulnerability to domestic abuse?

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: The domestic-abuse concession covers some spousal visa holders, but many victims are on other visas or have been made overstayers by abusers. They risk destitution, homelessness and returning to abusers because status and access to funds are cut off.

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: Women may also pick up debt from economic abuse or face false accusations that leave them with criminal records; both can bar settlement under the new tests. The result: a two-tier system that excludes many victims.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: The Government allows household income pooling to meet thresholds—does that help women with caring responsibilities?

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: Pooling helps some couples, but single parents and women who take time out to care remain exposed. The policy also risks keeping victims in abusive relationships to meet income tests, which is dangerous.

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: The 'best years' idea allows only a small number of low-earning years. Two children born close together, caring for disabled relatives or long-term sickness will easily push someone below thresholds, so the protections are limited.

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: The violence against women strategy cannot be delivered if migrant victims are excluded. Either exempt vulnerable groups from earned settlement or the strategy's aims are incompatible with these immigration changes.

chapters.title: Children, care leavers and the private-life routes
chapters.takeaway: Longer routes harm children's stability and future prospects; witnesses call for child-centred rules, clearer parental routes and a full child-rights impact assessment.

turns.speaker: Kevin McKenna
turns.text: Anita, what are the main harms for children when families face long temporary status?

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: Children need permanence to recover and plan. Long routes mean unstable housing and family income, worse school outcomes and barriers to university, apprenticeships or public-sector jobs that require settled status.

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: We welcome some five-year protections—long-resident children, some families of British children and unaccompanied minors—but many children as dependants will still be on long or indefinite pathways tied to parents' income and status.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: How do the private-life seven-year rules interact with these refugee and earned-settlement changes?

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: It's unclear. Current rules say some children can secure ILR after seven years or five years in certain cases, but where parents are on 20–30 year routes the family picture becomes complex. We want children to be able to settle with their first parent who becomes settled.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What about children in care or care leavers?

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: The Government has promised a pathway, but it isn't codified. We want a clear, fast, codified route for care-experienced children, and to extend protections like independent child trafficking guardians to support vulnerable young people into their mid-20s.

chapters.title: Refugees, asylum routes and criminality tests
chapters.takeaway: Refugees face much longer routes; penalties for irregular entry, debt and past convictions risk pushing people into destitution and exploitation.

turns.speaker: Richard Quigley
turns.text: What is the effect of 20 or 30-year routes for refugees?

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: Recognised refugees used to get five years then settle. Now the default is 'core protection' with repeated 30-month renewals and settlement after 20 years; irregular entry often adds time, so many face 30 years. Resettlement schemes remain narrow exceptions.

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: Asylum can't be claimed from abroad, so people take dangerous journeys. Penalising mode of arrival, debt for accommodation, criminality and restrictions on public funds combine to punish those who sought sanctuary.

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: For refugee children, long timelines damage identity and education. Families on long routes are less able to build stable employment and housing, which undermines their ability to 'earn' settlement even if the Government says it wants refugees to contribute.

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: The changes also interact with the Immigration and Asylum Bill: charges for state accommodation and wider measures mean refugees may acquire debt that blocks settlement under the new tests.

chapters.title: Practical impacts, costs, legal support and recommendations
chapters.takeaway: The proposals will increase legal complexity, demand for advice, costs for families and employers, and strain charities—witnesses call for impact assessments, exemptions and legal aid.

turns.speaker: Alex Brewer
turns.text: How will prolonged temporary status affect workers, employers and the care sector?

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: Employers face extra cost and churn. Example: an engineering firm with 120 skilled workers would see millions in extra visa costs. Care sector wages and the single-sponsor tie remain key issues for retention and exploitation risk.

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: Families have to save thousands for ILR fees. People choose between basics and applications; that pressures mental health and children’s prospects. Sliding fees or legal-cost supports would help.

turns.speaker: Nadia Whittome
turns.text: How will the 'by and for' women's organisations cope?

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: They are underfunded. Demand will rise but the sector can't hire migrant staff if thresholds bar them, so services and specialist lived-experience workers will shrink while need grows.

turns.speaker: Andrea Als
turns.text: Legal aid is severely limited. There will be a sharp rise in complex immigration cases—funding advice and protecting practitioners' safety online and offline should be priorities.

turns.speaker: Kevin McKenna
turns.text: What concrete steps should the Government take?

turns.speaker: Anita Hurrell
turns.text: Publish a full child-rights impact assessment and a Home Office child-impact assessment; codify a care-leaver pathway; let children settle with the first parent who gains settled status; soften criminality and debt bars for young people.

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: Exclude migrant victims of gender-based violence, children and other vulnerable groups from earned settlement rules; align immigration policy with the violence-against-women strategy and human-rights obligations.

turns.speaker: Sabrina Galella
turns.text: Demand that the Government publish full impact assessments (including equality and fiscal impacts) with the rules, and reverse retrospective changes that break legitimate expectations.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Any final points?

turns.speaker: Dr Siddiqui
turns.text: Retrospectivity destroys trust. If the UK wants people to integrate and feel British, it must keep promises, protect the vulnerable and remove reservations that prevent obligations under conventions like the Istanbul convention.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you to all witnesses for detailed evidence; the Committee will follow up on impact assessments, protections for children and victims, and the effects on legal and charity services.
